catalog_quote: 10.0 Stress is not phonemically significant and to a large extent subject to variation: yáki or yakí 'mountain goat', mác̓i or mac̓í 'cured salmon eggs'. In sonant- and V-less words stress is, of course, totally absent. 10.1 In certain environments there is, however, little variety concerning the place of stress: (a) it usually falls on the last V in the position -T≠: k°ułík 'roof', t̓amás 'cockle', ta_ƛ̓mstá_tx̌ 'the man'; (b) if a word contains a vocalic sonant or one following a V, the stress is, in general, attracted by the V, c.q. automatic schwa immediately preceding that R: max̌°at̓álaqa 'dipper (bird)', łmkm̓áni 'weasel', yulḿta 'spinning wool instrument'; (c) if a word contains two or more R's following a V, the stress will be fixed on the V before the last sonant but one: nuʔayawálsmaw 'they cleaned the house', ƛ̓mstáliwa 'self-supporting', q°ʼúnsxiwa 'whiteman'; (d) long V's tend to attract stress: łáax̌ałta 'shoulderblade', sq°áax̌q°a 'bullhead', q°úux̌°úux̌ 'swan'; (e) in the surrounding V/R Tf Tp V≠ it is the V or R directly preceding Tf that is stressed: slúxta 'crosspiece', ƛ̓lústa 'curtain', ƛ̓m̓ísta 'person'; (f) the final i (ii) in diminutive formations is always accented.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Bella Coola has no phonemic (distinctive) word stress; placement varies freely in many words (yáki ~ yakí) and all-obstruent words carry none. Phonetic prominence shows tendencies: the last vowel before word-final obstruent(s) (T = obstruent, ≠ = word border); the vowel before the second-to-last sonant when several sonants follow; long vowels attract stress; .V-fricative-stop-V# the vowel before the fricative; diminutive final -i always stressed. Newman 1947:132 independently states there are 'no phonemically significant phenomena of stress or pitch', with a variable high stressed tone on the last vowel or syllabic consonant before a pause.
new_statements.exceptions: Vowel-less/sonant-less words have no stress at all; diminutive final -i(i) always accented (Nater); Newman notes an optional falling-tone + final-high accent in diminutives that proved unstable across speakers.
new_statements.domain_note: Nater treats word + clitics as the stress domain (note 2: clitics 'play a decisive role in determining stress'); Newman's only regularity is pre-pausal (phrase-level: high stressed tone on last syllabic before pause). Both are impressionistic, no instrumental data. The reference grammar Nater 1984 pp. 27-28 (not opened) reportedly restates 'lack of distinctive stress' (per Nater 2013:123).
new_statements.identity_note: All sources describe Bella Coola / Nuxalk proper (bell1243); no dialect split. Nater 1978 is the conference pre-version of Nater 1979 (Lingua 49) and was later absorbed into Nater 1984 pp. 27-28.

sources.citation: Newman, Stanley. 1947. Bella Coola I: Phonology. IJAL 13(3):129-134 (sec. 3.3, p. 132).
sources.note: p.132: 'no phonemically significant phenomena of stress or pitch associated with syllables or words'; relative stresses do not remain constant in repetitions; 'A high stressed tone is generally pronounced on the last vowel or syllabic consonant before a pause, but this is a variable speech habit'; diminutive accent optional; 'no distinctive suprasegmental phonemes involving stress or pitch'.

sources.note: p.417: 'Oowekyala, like Bella Coola, lacks distinctive stress or tone'; p.419 endorses and block-quotes Newman 1947:132 ('no phonemically significant phenomena of stress or pitch').
